Some people might not know this but there used to be a site called Digg. You would "digg" a story you liked and a content stream was created based on these votes.

Well, around this time the encryption key for HD-DVD, a now defunct competitor to Blu-Ray, was published. As this key spread around the internet cease and desist letters were sent out. Thats right, they were claiming they owned essentially a random collection of 128 bits that happened to be the encryption key for HD-DVD.

The internet didn't take too kindly to that and one of the places this key was republished was Digg. The Digg staff decided that they would listen to the DMCA request and started banning anyone who shared this key. This resulted in an absolutely hilarious 24-72 hour period when every top story on Digg included the key in some way or another.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AACS_encryption_key_controversy#DMCA_notices_and_Digg

It was during that period when I heard of a site called Reddit. Every comment on a submission was being spammed with Reddit being the new "go to" place for censorship free discussion. Collectively the community gave a giant middle finger to Digg and abandoned ship. That truly was the beginning of the end for Digg which struggled over many months and years to regain its former glory. If you check digg.com now you'll see what looks like nothing more than a spammy content aggregator which might have ads for acaii berry weight loss solutions in the margins.

Sad to say it appears that Reddit has now followed in Digg's foot steps. Censorship should never be tolerated and Reddit has been given a longer run than than it honestly deserved.

Here we are again.... to those of you who might have felt Reddit was the first, know that it wasn't the first nor will it be the last, and be ready to leave Voat when the time inevitably comes that the sheer population size will warrant that "extra touch" from the powers that be. Know to recognize the writing on the wall and keep close those who see it with you.

I think you have to get some perspective. You talk about a very narrow range of for-profit companies that are all about popularity. Digg and reddit are anything but rare and uknown. There are thousands and thousands of forums out there.

Many sites offer more freedom because they don't plaster everything for Google and Bing search engines to see. They are more organized and specialized in their topics.

If you want to be deeply serious about openness - the Internet really isn't that expensive to publish on. Compared to printing books or mailing out postal letters. It's very cheap. But still, people rely heavily on advertising for funding - or if the site does well - they sell it off (just like reddit did). It's well within the means of the average person to pay for a text-only site that supports a few thousand users.

Monolithic run-by-one group systems are not going to lead to free speech and openness over the long term. There are no checks and balances. People don't have established paths in case of an emergency, etc. Digg and Reddit communities were mostly not very serious in actually setting up alternate sites, etc. Lots of bitching, but very little discussion of creating alternates - and how relatively easy it is on the technical side. Just like newspapers and their comment communities, it's mostly about profits and popularity.

Usenet is one of the oldest things on the Internet - and it was fully distributed. It wasn't centralized and managed by a corporation. The protocols and technology for text peer to peer conversation have been there - and could be modernized pretty easily. Bitching just seems more popular. People don't seem to want to come together to solve it. You can Kickstarter a movie or TV show reboot, but people don't want to actually create a non-profit open-source text discussion website. Reddit's Python code is open source - very few bother to set it up and run on Linux.
